Chapter 03

CSS: the paint

Selectors, the box model, the cascade, and custom properties — the four ideas that explain almost everything CSS does.

By the end of this chapter

You will read CSS confidently and understand why our styling is organised the way it is.

CSS answers: which elements, and what should they look like? Every rule has the same shape.

  • h1 is the selector — which elements this applies to.
  • Everything in the braces is the declaration block.
  • color is a property; white is its value. Each pair ends with a semicolon.

Selectors

A class is a label you put on elements: <div class="card">. You can use the same class on as many elements as you like, and one element can have several. Classes are the workhorse of CSS.

The box model

Every element is a rectangle with four layers, from the inside out:

  • Content — the text or image itself.
  • Padding — space *inside* the box, between the content and the border. Background colour extends through it.
  • Border — a line around the padding.
  • Margin — space *outside* the box, pushing other elements away. Always transparent.

Padding or margin?

Padding is space the element owns — it makes the element itself bigger. Margin is space between this element and its neighbours. If you want a button to feel roomier, that is padding. If you want two buttons further apart, that is margin.

By default, width: 300px means the *content* is 300px, and any padding and border are added on top — so your 300px box is actually 340px and your layout breaks. border-box makes width mean the whole box, which is what everyone assumes it means. It is not the default only for historical reasons. Put this in every project.

The cascade: which rule wins

CSS stands for *Cascading* Style Sheets. When two rules target the same element, the conflict is settled in this order:

  1. Specificity. A more specific selector wins. An id (#main) beats a class (.card), which beats an element (p).
  2. Order. If specificity ties, whichever comes later in the file wins.
  3. !important. Overrides everything. Almost always a sign something has gone wrong — you are fighting your own stylesheet.

This project writes !important exactly three times, all in one place: the reduced-motion kill-switch in reset.css, which must override every animation on the site no matter how specific the selector that set it — the one canonical legitimate use. If you reach for it anywhere else, the real problem is usually a selector that is more specific than it needs to be somewhere else.

Custom properties (CSS variables)

You can store a value and reuse it. This is the single most important CSS feature for keeping a large project coherent.

  • A custom property must start with two dashes: --name.
  • :root means the whole document — define them there and they are available everywhere.
  • var(--name) reads the value back.

Why this matters so much

Change --brand-blue in one place and every button, link and border using it updates. Without variables, changing a brand colour means find-and-replacing a hex code across fifty files, missing three, and creating a site where two blues are almost-but-not-quite the same. Chapter 12 builds our entire design system out of these.

Units

  • px — pixels. Fixed. Fine for borders, bad for text.
  • rem — relative to the browser's base font size (normally 16px, so 1rem = 16px). Use this for text and spacing. If a user increases their default font size for readability, rem respects it and px ignores it.
  • em — relative to the *current element's* font size. Useful for spacing that should scale with its own text.
  • % — relative to the parent.
  • vw / vh — 1% of the viewport width / height.
  • ch — the width of a 0 character. max-width: 70ch caps a paragraph at about 70 characters, which is the readable range.

Use rem rather than px for font sizes. Setting text in px overrides a user's accessibility settings — for someone with low vision who has increased their default size, your site simply ignores them. It is also a WCAG failure.

Flexbox and Grid, briefly

Two layout systems. You will use both, and the rule of thumb is simple.

Flexbox for a row or a column — one direction. Grid when you need rows *and* columns. gap works in both and is far better than putting margins on children, because it never leaves a stray margin on the last item.
